nodes.name: General Staff
nodes.unit_type: Drawn from all service components; promulgates policy, supervises service components; merges with MOD to form SHC in wartime

notes: Peacetime: MOD and General Staff operate closely but separately (MOD = policy/acquisitions/financing; General Staff = policy promulgation + service supervision via functional directorates). Wartime: MOD+General Staff merge into Supreme High Command (SHC), a unified headquarters under the Chief of the General Staff (CGS). SID coordinates (dashed lines) all State ministries per national security strategy, particularly those tied to the four instruments of national power (diplomatic-political, informational, economic, military).

Text explicitly cross-refs FM/TC 7-100.4 for the basic organic/administrative-force-structure (AFS) organization of these services -- TC 7-100.2's contribution is the strategic C2 framework layered above, not a duplicate of 7-100.4 unit structures. Administrative Force Structure (AFS, para 1-6/1-7) is the peacetime grouping (corps/armies/army groups/military regions/districts) that differs from the wartime fighting force structure (Field Group / OSC / DTG-BTG, see employment notes) -- administrative HQs act as force providers that transfer major units to task-organized fighting commands in wartime.

name: Counterreconnaissance Detachment (CRD)

nodes.name: CRD
nodes.unit_type: Counterreconnaissance Detachment -- task organization created specifically for the counterreconnaissance (CR) mission

notes: Example organization only -- CRD components vary per mission (para 6-18): reconnaissance elements (long-range recon units, mounted/dismounted combat recon, signals recon, aerial recon, or SPF -- the most essential component), air defense (defensive protection of the CRD OR offensive use against enemy UAVs/recon aircraft/helicopters), aviation (rapid infantry transport to located targets, armed/unarmed recon, resupply), artillery (kills recon without direct-fire engagement, precision systems preferred to avoid endangering other OPFOR forces in battle/support zones). Each CRZ (counterreconnaissance zone, a CRD's AOR, subdivision of the disruption zone or larger AOR) is the responsibility of exactly one CRD. CRD may absorb the security force's mission entirely, or operate alongside a separate security force (para 6-17).

nodes.name: Artillery Component (optional -- dashed box in source)

Missile Component (optional -- dashed box in source)

Integrated Support Group (optional -- dashed box in source)
nodes.unit_type: Sustainment -- one of the division/DTG's ISGs, supporting the IFC specifically (see ch14 ISC/ISG)

notes: All component boxes dashed in source = present per mission requirements, NOT a fixed TOE (para 9-25: 'The IFC is not organized according to a table of organization and equipment, but is task-organized to accomplish the missions assigned'). Every division/DTG-level org ALWAYS has an IFC C2 structure (staff, CP, comms/intel architecture, automated fire control system/AFCS) even with zero additional fire-support units attached (para 9-21). No IFC exists below division/DTG -- brigades/BTGs have a 'chief of fire support coordination' staff element instead (ch2). IFC commander = the division/DTG Deputy Commander (DC); can also be given command of maneuver forces (disruption force, exploitation force) when tightly coordinated fires are required.

notes: Example only (para 10-10/10-11): IFC may be organized to include an army aviation component for attack/DAS/reconnaissance missions plus CSS helicopters for troop movement, resupply, C2 platforms. Command/support relationship to the IFC depends on mission type/available assets/duration -- continuous lift needs = constituent/dedicated; one-time troop movement = supporting relationship, helicopter battalion stays under its parent aviation unit's control instead of joining the IFC. Cross-references ch2 and ch9 for full IFC detail.

nodes.unit_type: Staff section -- requisition/acquisition/distribution/care of all command resources (human and materiel); at battalion level the resources officer also performs chief-of-administration duties, and the materiel support platoon leader serves as chief of logistics

nodes.name: Logistics Subsection
nodes.unit_type: Manages supply order/receipt/distribution; maintains combat readiness of armaments/equipment

nodes.name: Administration Subsection
nodes.unit_type: Supervises personnel actions/transactions: daily strength reports, TOE change records (AFS), personnel assignment, replacement requests, loss records, awards/decorations, war booty disposition

notes: Division/brigade-level staff section (secondary staff under the Resources Officer, see htfs_dtg_division_command_staff / htfs_battalion_command_staff for the full staff org this sits inside).

name: Integrated Support Command (ISC) Headquarters

nodes.name: Integrated Support Command HQ
nodes.unit_type: Provides C2/admin/ops/support personnel and equipment forming the nucleus of the division's two Integrated Support Groups (ISGs)

nodes.name: ISC Staff / COS
nodes.unit_type: Staff, headed by Chief of Staff

nodes.name: Commander
nodes.unit_type: ISC Commander -- division logistician; advises division commander/resources officer/staff

nodes.name: Operations Section
nodes.unit_type: Contains the Support Operations Coordination Center (SOCC), where the RISTA and INFOWAR officer resides

nodes.name: Support Operations Coordination Center (SOCC)
nodes.unit_type: Planning/coordination of support for the division and IFC; RISTA and INFOWAR officer resides here

nodes.name: Liaison Teams (multiple, not permanent, dashed box)
nodes.unit_type: Not a permanent part of ISC staff; provide subject-matter expertise + direct comms to subordinate/supporting units; may come from multinational/interagency/affiliated forces; provide own equipment

nodes.name: Tactical Security Section
nodes.unit_type: Security -- general security for the sustainment CP(s)

notes: For additional detail on ISC organization, text explicitly cross-references FM 7-100.4 (para 14-26) -- confirms this pub's ISC HQ chart is a task-org overlay, not a duplicate TOE. ISC commander/staff task-organize the two ISGs (one supporting the division, one supporting the IFC) based on mission requirements -- see htfs_dtg_isg_example for a worked ISG example.

name: DTG Integrated Support Group (ISG), example

nodes.name: Integrated Support Group
nodes.unit_type: Compilation of support-task units (primarily logistics; may also include engineer, chemical warfare, law enforcement, RISTA, INFOWAR tasks) -- one of the division's two ISGs (this example supports a DTG not relying on extensive parent-OSC support)

nodes.name: Personnel Service Battalion
nodes.unit_type: Sustainment (personnel services) -- drawn in source spanning below both the traffic control and medical battalions jointly

notes: EXAMPLE ONLY (para 14-31): 'Figure 14-3 is one example of a rather robust ISG that might be appropriate for a DTG not relying on extensive support from a parent OSC.' No standard ISG organizational structure exists (para 14-30) -- number/type/mix of subordinate elements varies by tactical support situation; ISG has six major functions regardless of exact org: supply, maintenance, transportation, medical support, personnel services, field services (may also do engineer/chemical/law-enforcement/RISTA/INFOWAR tasks). The second-tier battalions (Smoke, Traffic Control, Medical, Evacuation, Personnel Service) are drawn in the source hanging below the four first-tier brigade/battalion boxes at natural nearest-neighbor positions -- parent_ref assignments here follow the visual column position, not a doctrinal command statement; treat this figure as illustrative task organization, not fixed TOE.

The parallel TC 7-100.4 extraction pass (extraction_ledger_tc71004.json, chunk tc71004_chunk_0001/0002) found only a CATALOG-ONLY listing for 'Special-Purpose Forces (SPF) Brigade' in TC 7-100.4 Appendix A (name + component list, no reproduced chart) -- so this TC 7-100.2 figure is currently the ONLY charted version of the SPF brigade structure across both extraction passes; do not treat as a duplicate to discard. nodes.unit_type: Special-Purpose Forces -- overt/covert/clandestine attacks: assassination, abduction/hostage-taking, sabotage, capture, ambush, raid

nodes.name: SPF Team (Sapper)
nodes.unit_type: Special-Purpose Forces (engineer/raider) -- assault of fixed installations, IED/booby-trap manufacture and emplacement, mine warfare/demolition

notes: CROSS-REFERENCE per para 15-32 (FM 7-100.4 provenance, see htfs_spf_brigade_example). Example showing a company with at least one of each specialized team type (para 15-53) -- alternate composition example given in text (not charted): 'four standard SPF teams, one direct action team, one air infiltration team, one sniper team, one medical team, one signal team, and one sapper team.' A company may instead be single-focus (all teams the same specialty) or any mix. All SPF members are cross-trained on the full range of specialty capabilities regardless of team label (para 15-52/15-53 area).

name: Commando Brigade (example)

nodes.name: INFOWAR Company
nodes.unit_type: Information Warfare -- peculiar to commando brigade

notes: Example only (para 15-177): 'A commando brigade will generally need to be task-organized to meet specific mission requirements and conditions, in which case it becomes a commando BTG.' Could easily also include an engineer battalion (civil affairs), an artillery and/or MRL battalion or battery, an SPF battalion or company, affiliated irregular forces, or a helicopter company. Cross-reference: 'other brigade subordinates are organized and function similar to their counterparts in regular ground forces organizations' (para 15-181) -- long-range signal company/materiel support company/medical platoon are the SAME support-unit types as in htfs_spf_brigade_example, not commando-specific; recon company and INFOWAR company are described as 'peculiar to a commando brigade' (para 15-181).

nodes.name: Maintenance Section
nodes.unit_type: Sustainment (maintenance) -- tests/diagnostic checks/repairs/maintenance on parachutes, ultralight aircraft, support systems, related equipment

notes: Ultralights may be armed (light/general-purpose machineguns, AGLs, ATDLs) or fitted with radios/cameras/sensor sets/laser target designators; used in attack, reconnaissance, or multimission roles, not just infiltration (note, para 15-179). Dismantled two-per-trailer for transport. For additional info, text cross-references FM 7-100.4 (para 15-180).
